utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Hannis, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, only because I was afraid I'd disappear out of sight behind the podium if I sat down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not easily out of sight, Mr. Hannis. Is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a witness without any protective measures in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's Mr. Crncalo. I hope the pronunciation is good enough to understand whom we are talking about. But first of all, Madam Registrar, I would like you to call the case, because I've forgotten to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. And is it you, Mr. Hannis, who will examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I say at this moment good morning, Witness, because I see that your name is spelled differently in several statements. But we'll hear about the correct name and the spelling of it, and perhaps the pronunciation later. Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And the text of this declaration will be handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll hear soon, I take it, Mr. Hannis, whether Mr. Sulejman Crncalo or Crncajlo. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning. Just to help us -- good morning, Mr. Crncalo. To help us out, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- how you spell your last name.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Crncalo and my first name is Sulejman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you spell your last name for us.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: C-r-n-c-a-l-o.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Your Honour, I would like to begin by showing the witness his two statements. His ICTY statement of 8 June 2001, I would ask that that be marked as the next exhibit. And his statement to the high court in Sarajevo, dated 23 August 1995, to be the following exhibit. And if he could be shown both at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement dated 8th of June, 2001 is P270 and the record of witness interview of 23rd August 1995, P271.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the ICTY witness statement, the original would be English, and for the High Court statement, the original would be in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I would ask you first to look at the document that's a statement to the High Court in Sarajevo in August 1995. Do you see that one?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's a name on the first page that appears very similar to yours, but the last name is spelled slightly different. Can you tell us whether the person that's being talked about there is you and it's simply a misspelling of your name, or is that some other person?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: This is my family name misspelled. The order of letters A and C is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But do you recognise the signature at the bottom of each of the pages on that document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to look at that statement yesterday and read it over before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, at the very end of the day I had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to look at the other statement that's on the table before you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. I had a look at the other statement too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you able to read both of those fully and satisfy yourself that those indeed were statements that you had made on those previous occasions as dated on those documents?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. I read both statements and both of them are the statements that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And apart from a couple of very minor things that we talked about yesterday, can you confirm to this Court that both those statements were true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief at the time you made them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I can confirm what is written in the statements when I made them. I made a small addition yesterday, but apart from that, I stand behind my statements, and you can ask me anything you want regarding these two statements, and I'm perfectly willing to answer all your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would indicate to the Court, I think I've sent to Mr. De Hemptinne in your Chambers and to Defence counsel a supplemental information sheet regarding some of the new items that came up in our proofing session and there are a couple of typographical errors in the English version of his ICTY statement that I would point out to the Court when we come to those as I go through the statement with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With that in mind, Your Honour, I would propose to read a summary of his statements at this time, if I may do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 89(F) summary. Yes. We have not received yet the summary. I take it that it was communicated to the Defence. And yes, then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I believe copies have been provided to the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the summary of the prior statements of Mr. Crncalo. The witness was a Muslim factory worker who lived in Pale from 1978 until the time he was expelled on 2 July 1992. He describes the persecution of Muslims in Pale from 1991 until July 1992, when almost all the remaining Muslims were transferred out of the municipality, and the participation of the Bosnian Serb forces (including, in particular, the police, acting in cooperation with paramilitary units) in this campaign. He describes meetings that he and other Muslim representatives had with Serb officials, including the chief of police, Malko Koroman, and one meeting with a member of the Bosnian Serb collective Presidency, Nikola Koljevic, regarding the persecutions and involuntary transfer of Muslims from Pale. Mr. Crncalo states that during 1991 to early 1992 he noted: Increased public manifestation of nationalism by the Serb majority living in Pale, in particular, a May 1991 ceremony by V. Seselj; the distribution of weapons to the local Serb population, and the mobilisation of his Serb coworkers. In response, the Muslim community felt threatened and started guarding their households. On 3 March 1992, the witness was arrested by Serb reserve policemen while guarding his house, taken to the local Pale police station, handcuffed, interrogated by police, threatened with death and beaten for three hours. Mr. Crncalo states that in the beginning of March 1992, the Crisis Staff for the municipality of Pale was established, and that it controlled all municipal activities. It was headquartered at the police headquarters and consisted of SDS leaders, including the SDS president, the chief of police, and the municipality president. The witness states that from March 1992, there was a public call over the television directed to all non-Serbs to surrender all weapons to the police; paramilitary men conducted searches of Muslim homes; Serbs (including, in particular, the police and a paramilitary unit commander, Radomir Kojic) started a campaign to have all non-Serbs leave Pale municipality; and checkpoints were established and manned by paramilitaries and reserve soldiers severely restricting movement of Muslims and cutting them off from neighbouring Muslim communities. During May 1992, he saw three civilian transport trucks full of civilian Muslim men from Bratunac arrive in Pale, escorted by Serb paramilitaries. The trucks stopped in front of the police station and the president of the municipality, Starcevic, came out and said that he did not have a place for all these prisoners. He directed that the Muslim men be taken to the nearby cinema. In April and May 1992, the Muslims' telephone service was cut off. Further, on 15 May 1992, the witness and his fellow Muslim co-workers were dismissed from work. During May-June 1992, he noticed increased concentrations of military equipment and military personnel in the Pale area, including hundreds of paramilitaries. From April there were random arrests of Muslims and in June and July several Muslim men were arrested in their homes by paramilitaries and killed. Finally, in late June and early July, the Serb authorities, in particular, the SDS Crisis Staff, organised convoys to remove Muslims from the area. After his and his family's removal on 2 July 1992, the witness learned that the three mosques in the Pale area were destroyed and the Muslims who had refused to leave the Pale area in July 1992 were killed. In May 1992, the witness and other Muslims asked the chief of police to organise a meeting with a competent authority so they could determine why the Serbs were forcing them to leave their homes. The meeting was to take place at the police station. When the Muslims arrived at the police station, they were told to go to a coffee bar owned by a Muslim, Fadil Kujovic. After approximately 10 minutes, Nikola Koljevic, accompanied by two active-duty policemen, Stanar and Jovicic, arrived. The witness was a member of the delegation, which explained that the Muslims did not want to leave their homes and wanted to live peacefully in Pale. Mr. Koljevic replied: "It does not matter that you want to live with us; the Serbs don't want to go on living with you." In addition to this meeting, the witness had a number of other meetings with Serb authorities, including the chief of police and one meeting with the president of the municipality, about why the police were forcing the Muslims to leave, and received various responses, including, on one occasion, a response from the police chief that he could not protect the Muslim population from paramilitaries. The witness also saw Radovan Karadzic in June 1992 during a public meeting near the police station in Pale. The evidence, Your Honour, is relevant to paragraphs 4, 8, 12, 19, 21, 22, and 27, and counts 3, 7, and 8 of the indictment. And that concludes my reading of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I want to ask you some questions about your statements, but I would ask you, to the extent that you can, if you can answer my questions from your present memory. If you need to refer to the statement, will you let us know that you're looking at the statement when you're making the answer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Go ahead. Ask me questions. I'll answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, sir, I'd like to just --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, sir, I would like to ask you -- well, first I would like to state a little bit about your background and ask you if that's correct and then I will ask you about some particular events in your statement. Mr. Crncalo, I believe it's correct that you were born and grew up in Pale municipality and that you were trained in metal working. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you did your mandatory military service in 1965 and 1966?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After the army, you worked for a company called the Zrak company, for about four years?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that, I don't believe it's in your statement, but did you work outside the country for some period of time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that in the Republic of Germany, until 1978?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, in Germany, in Munich. I returned in 1978. I returned home to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you returned in 1978, did you build a home and go to work at the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Famos, in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what kind of work did you do at Famos?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I was working on manufacturing tank parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us how big, how many people, approximately, lived in Pale municipality in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Up to the beginning of war, including all the villages in the entire territory of Pale, there were about 15.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many lived in the town of Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Approximately 5.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate breakdown of the three different ethnic groups within Pale municipality in 1991, 1992, before the war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, but a very little per cent of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate percentage of Serbs and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: According to what I know, I can talk about two different percentages. I didn't have direct insight into the breakup of the population. I learned from others what the situation was before the war. According to some information, there were 28 per cent of Muslims. According to some other sources, there were 33 per cent of Muslims. I can't account for the 5 per cent difference. I don't know where the difference comes from between 33 and 28 per cent. There were about 5 per cent Croats and the rest of the population were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand from your statement that you were not a member of any political party, nor active in politics; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your ICTY statement in 2001, you talked about -- you noticed a change beginning in 1991 in the municipality, with more focus on nationalism. And I want to ask you in particular about paragraph 11 in your ICTY statement. You make reference to the 6th of May, 1991 and an event regarding a Serb holiday. Do you recall that event?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I do, indeed. I remember the event very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what that was about, how you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In the territory of Pale municipality, there is a mountain called Romanija. This is a mythical mountain. According to this myth, this is where Hajduks, Serbian heroes, lived. On the mountain of Romanija, there is a cave which used to serve as the hiding-place of Starina Novak, a Serb Hajduk. This cave has always been mentioned in Serb myths as a good place, and Starina Novak has always been mentioned as a hero, the biggest hero of the time. That year on the date that is mentioned in my statement, Seselj was rumoured to be visiting the cave on the 6th of May. According to tradition, the 6th of May is the day when Hajduks used to gather in nature, that is, in the mountain. Most probably, Seselj wanted to revive this tradition. At the beginning of his political career, Seselj established his Radical Party. 90 per cent of the programme of this party, according to what I know, was to establish the so-called Chetnik formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, Mr. Crncalo, and ask you a question. What was the source of your information about some event happening on this day involving Mr. Seselj? How did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We heard about it -- I don't know. The story came to us that Seselj would be coming to Novak's cave for some sort of meeting or rally of his party. And as soon as we heard about that, the arrival of Seselj, we knew where the wind was blowing, what his party and their supporters, the direction they were going in. And we thought that there would be a lot of drinking, that they would be drunk, and they were radicals, and if they had some alcohol to drink, then they could cause chaos and crimes among the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know if there was such a gathering on the 6th of May, 1991, at that location?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, there was a gathering like that, and at the end of the gathering - and I haven't ever stated this before, but there we are. I've just remembered it, and that is that he used a horse when he went back and he was going back, and he fell off the horse and injured his face, and his men, if I can put it that way, or his supporters in the villages that he rode through, they were members of his party, and they joked and said that Seselj injured his head while conducting the meeting in Novak's cave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You referred earlier to the term "Chetniks." Can you tell the Court what you're referring to when you use that term. I assume you're not referring to all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The people who opted and chose this kind of paramilitary formation were ultraradicals, and they had their traditions, and on one occasion I saw -- rather, the Serbs showed me themselves, at a petrol station, when I was waiting to tank up, I saw two men wearing black clothes that were handmade from handmade textiles and they were trousers and a shirt, and they had some insignia on their sleeves. But I wasn't able to see that properly or recognise it. And they had a large fur hat on their heads, called the subara, and with the crossed bones insignia and skull, skull and crossbones insignia on that hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there something about this gathering and the increased nationalism that caused you and your Muslim neighbours any concerns?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, we had to be concerned, knowing what we did, because in World War I and World War II, we knew what the paramilitary formations did to the non-Serbs, whether they were Croats or Muslims. And we felt that they could do the same thing in this latest war. So yes, we were afraid. Had to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us what that was that you were concerned about that had been done in World War I and World War II.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In those two wars, wherever the Chetnik formations arrived, there was mass suffering of Muslims or Croats. Although these units, these formations, didn't have access to ethnically pure Croatian communities. In fact, those formations were usually rampant in the eastern part of Bosnia. Mostly. I can't say 100 per cent and I can't guarantee that they didn't go to other parts at times, Herzegovina, for example, western Herzegovina, but to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In May of 1991, when this event was happening, did you and your neighbours do anything in response because of your concerns?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did try to do something. We tried to observe the streets and the approaches to the houses, and for a time that's what I did, until I was arrested. When I was arrested, then we stopped this vigilance. We weren't able to stand in front of the houses and observe the surrounding area from that area. But we would be inside the houses, two or three families would group together inside the houses and stay awake, unless we were gathered together; then you would have whole families disappear in these terrible nights. During the day it was a little easier. You could see better if somebody was coming towards your house or passing by in the street. And anyway, there were a lot of unknown people walking around during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me jump ahead for a minute and ask you a chronological question. When were you arrested while standing guard outside your house?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: On the 3rd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us that -- I think you said that -- or perhaps it's in your statement, that you began standing guard duty outside your homes around the 6th of May, 1991, when this event involving Mr. Seselj occurred. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you and your Muslim neighbours continue to stand guard duty every night from May 1991 through March 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't. While Seselj went on the 6th of May to Novak's cave and returned, that same night, in the patrol, I was found in front of my house by a policeman called Milan Simovic, and he was controlling the municipality of Pale. And when he saw me standing in front of the house - and anyway, we had gone to school together - he said: Why aren't you sleeping? And he addressed me as a school friend. What's the reason? And I said: Well, we heard that Seselj was up at Romanija in Novak's cave, so we are rather afraid. We're afraid that something might happen to us. And his response was: Tonight, three local communities in our municipality are awake. They're not sleeping. Hrenovica, Podgrad and this area here at Pale, the Muslim part of Pale. After that, he said: You can go and get some sleep, and if anything is happening, you can call me and I'll come. So don't worry. We said goodbye to each other and he went on patrol. He continued his patrolling. But I didn't dare go to sleep nonetheless, and I stayed awake until daybreak, but nothing actually happened to us that time. Now, the period you're asking me about, about the guard duty, from 1991 to 1992, we did not stand guard duty all the time. For a month or so, during the month of May, I believe, we were on guard duty, but then as the tensions dropped and things became calmer, we stopped doing guard duty, until the demonstrations began, and that was sometime in 1992, after Christmas. Demonstrations for Kosovo, that Kosovo shouldn't be relinquished. And then we started guard duty again until I was arrested and taken into custody, when we stopped doing guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Now, you talked a little bit about the Chetniks and you mentioned in your statement, I think, in paragraph 14, about some of the local Serb -- you made a reference to local Serb Chetniks and their being armed. Do you have specific individuals in mind when you referred to the local Serb Chetniks? Was there a group of people that you can name or were they under the leadership of someone locally?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I said a moment ago that Seselj organised the Radical Party, and within that Radical Party, the members were those people who liked the Chetnik movement. But I can't actually give you any names because I wasn't able to recognise even the two men that I described a moment ago, whereas the other Serbs showed me, they called me, called out my name, and pointed to me and said: Sulejman, now you can see what Chetniks look like. Because up until then, I didn't have a chance to see what the clothing they wore looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately when was it when those two men were pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you an exact date, but I can give you the month. It was March. And there was a great shortage of fuel, and I went to the petrol station to tank up, and in the meantime the two of them arrived, as I said, and then they were pointed out to me. People pointed out these two men to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In March of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your ICTY statement, in paragraph 17, for the Court, you make reference to some distribution of weapons to the Serbs. And you talk about the involvement of a Stjepan Koroman in that activity, and you say that you were told about this by an Esad Basic. Can you tell the Court what Mr. Basic told you about this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Esad Basic is a close relative of mine and he lived in a village called Kamenica, near Jahorina, the mountain. And he set off for Pale one day, for some reason. He had a car. And on the way to Podrava [phoen], that is to say between Kamenica and Podrava, he happened to meet, as he described it to me at the time, a car that was like a small truck, with a cabin and the back part of the truck was covered with a tarpaulin. And as the village road was rather bumpy and there was a lot of rain, when the two cars met, as the road was bumpy, the car went up and down, balancing along the road, and part of the tarpaulin uncovered the back part of the truck and you could see the -- what the truck had inside. And when they were passing each other, these two cars, Esad's car must have hit a pool of water and sprinkled the truck with water. Both vehicles stopped. Stjepan Koroman came out of the truck and asked Esad why he had sprayed and dirtied his vehicle. And the other man didn't answer. But both of them, Esad Basic and Stjepan Koroman got out of their vehicles. When they met, Esad said that he saw that there were rifles loaded up onto the back of the truck. He could see that because part of the tarpaulin, part of the canvas covering the truck had become unhinged. And Stjepan told him, don't tell anyone what you've just seen. And he said that Stjepan was angry when he told him that. And that's what Esad told me about that encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he tell you what kind of rifles and how many there were?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, he didn't give a number, but he just said he saw that the back part of the small truck was half full and covered with the canvas, with the awning. And all the rifles were manufactured by the Crna Zastava red flag factory of Kragujevac. And they were easily visible and recognisable. All of us who had done our military service could recognise that type of rifle at a glance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what type of rifle is that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What type of rifle is that? Is that a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It's an army, a military, automatic rifle, which takes 30 bullets. It can fire a burst of gunfire or individual gunshots. And because they were such elegant rifles, we would call them gypsy women, and you could place an anti-aircraft device on each of these rifles. Rifle grenades could be attached to each of those rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the company you mentioned that manufactured these rifles, where is that located?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In Serbia, in the town of Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stjepan Koroman, was he related to any official who worked in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He had members of his family in political circles within the municipality, in Famos as well. Among one of the managers, and a closer relative was Malko Koroman, the head of the police department at Pale, police administration at Pale of the day, that is to say, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this was that Esad had seen these rifles?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That was the period from Christmas to March. It could have been February, actually. I'm not quite sure. Don't hold me to a date. But during that period of time, anyway, before the initial shelling of Sarajevo. And all the statements that came from Sarajevo that the war officially began on the 6th of April, I myself was able to see from the window of my house on the 5th of April, it was night, the night between Saturday and Sunday, and I heard how the shelling of Sarajevo started that night. I heard it start.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me stop you there, Mr. Crncalo. I want to ask you a further question about arming. In paragraph 18 you say it was "common knowledge to my community and me that the Serbs obtained weapons from several army barracks in the Pale area." Can you tell us how this was common knowledge? What was your source of information about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: When news travels through the population, you usually refer to that as being a public, an open secret. So it wasn't something that happened overnight. I heard many times from my colleagues at work, while we still went to work, I heard them asking each other: What were you given tonight or last night, and how many pieces were you issued? I didn't pay much attention to these questions and that kind of thing because I thought that as Christmas was almost upon us and Serbian holidays and religious holidays, I didn't pay much attention. But they said somebody got two rifles, another man got one rifle. So one person would complain about having been given an old rifle, dating back to World War II. The old type of rifle that you had to -- which wasn't automatic. You had to use your hand. It had to be opened manually. So they were complaining of having been issued rifles like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And which colleagues at work are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, my colleagues at work. We worked together in Famos. At work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were these colleagues of one particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. One particular ethnicity. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regarding your Serb colleagues at work in paragraph 19 of your ICTY statement, you indicated that in January 1992, your Serb co-workers began to be mobilised. Did no Muslim workers at Famos get mobilised?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: At that time, when it all began, when things began to happen, at work we had a plan that had to be implemented within one month, that is to say, we had to provide our buyers with the goods. But when the mobilisation started, there was not enough manpower, and the production plan began to stagnate, and we were discussing this amongst ourselves when the first tour of mobilisation took part. We wondered where all the people were, where the managers were, and they just shook their heads and said they didn't know. Because we said we'll be left without a salary. We're not able to meet our production plans. And then the next tour of mobilisation, the next bout started, and production levels dropped further. Everybody was being mobilised but not a single Muslim. And on one occasion, coming back from work, I happened to recognise somebody I knew very well, Nedeljko Vukovic, a colleague of mine from work. He was wearing a uniform, standing beside some sort of vehicle. And I asked -- I called him Neso, and I said to him: Neso what are you doing there? And he said: Well, I've been mobilised. And I said where. Well, he says, I'm driving something to Capljina. And he had been issued a vehicle, a military vehicle which was referred to as a Campagnola.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be useful we suggest, with respect, if Your Honour could give this witness one of Your Honour's occasional reminders that the question that is put by counsel is what he should answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, may I ask you to carefully listen to the question and to answer to that question, and if any further details are of importance for us, Mr. Hannis will certainly ask you about that. And Mr. Hannis, you could perhaps lead the witness in that respect a bit more. We are under some time constraints, and of course I know that you have a lot to tell us, but Mr. Hannis, Prosecution, and Defence might be interested in very specific points. So would you first answer that, and if any further information is needed, we'll certainly ask you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I'll try to get to the point I wanted to clear up with you. You said Serb co-workers were being mobilised during this time period; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were any Muslims, any of your Muslim co-workers at the Famos factory mobilised during this time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to be clear about that, because we know that in some parts of Bosnia, there were mobilisation calls in which Muslims were called up, but simply refused to go. And I want to find out if in Pale, in Famos factory, your Muslim co-workers, was it a case of they got call-ups and refused to go or they simply did not get called up? If you know.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Simply, they didn't get a call-up for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me ask you this question, first of all, if you can answer yes or no. Do you have an opinion about whether Muslims could have joined up and mobilised if they had volunteered themselves without being called, in Pale? Yes or no. Do you have an opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, you have no opinion, or your opinion is: No, they could not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, they couldn't have been called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's the basis for your opinion to that effect? Was there some incident that gave you an opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There were no such cases, and if I can explain, if I may be allowed to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could explain briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I will do. When there is a mobilisation, first there is -- officers are mobilised and they're followed by soldiers, and this is what did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And when you had been in the army or the reserves, were you an officer?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go forward now. I want to go to what you have mentioned before in March of 1992, when you were guarding your home. You told us you were arrested that night. Can you tell us briefly how that happened? Who arrested you? Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I was standing in front of my house. All of a sudden, three policemen appeared. All three pointed their rifles at me. They handcuffed me and they marched me to the police station. My hunting rifle was leaning against the house wall. I did not hold it in my hands. However, they picked the rifle up and took it to the police station. Shall I now tell you what happened to me in the police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some specific questions about it. And this may help you to realise that your statements, your written statements from before, have been marked as exhibits and we're going to offer those as evidence to the Court. So the Court, if they haven't already read that, will be reading that. So we don't need to tell them about everything that's written down there. I want to try and fill in some of the gaps. The three policemen who arrested you, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know, were they local Serbs? Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They were reserve policemen. I didn't know them. None of them. As for their accent, it appeared that they came from the same neck of woods, from the same part of Bosnia. However, I did not recognise any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your written statement, you describe how you were taken to the police station and interrogated and beaten by an individual named Hrsum. What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: His family name was Hrsum and his ethnic origin was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what -- was he a member of the Pale police department, a regular policeman as opposed to a reserve policeman?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was a member of the reserve police. I apologise. I'm sorry. Were you referring to the ones that arrested me or the one that interrogated me, Hrsum? I gave my answer maybe too quickly, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. You told us before that the reserve policemen were Serbs. I was asking you about Mr. Hrsum, whether he was a reserve or a regular policeman.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was a regular policeman, an inspector in the crime prevention police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your statement, you describe what you went through there at the police station, but I want to ask you about what happened later in that evening or in the morning, early morning hours, when Malko Koroman came in. When he arrived, did you talk to him about what had happened to you before he got there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I was standing in the hallway. My hands were still handcuffed. When Malko entered the police station, he recognised me and asked me: What are you doing here? And I answered that he should talk to his policemen about that. He invited me to go with him to the room that he was entering. A neighbour of mine had already been there. Hrsum was interrogating him as I came to the door. He ordered Hrsum to leave the room. Hrsum obeyed him. Then he invited me in and he asked me to sit down on a chair. Malko asked me: How come the police arrested me in front of my house? How come his policemen found themselves in my street? I answered: I don't know how it happened. You should ask them. And then he pointed to his automatic rifle that he brought with him and he also pointed to the hunting rifles that belonged to me and to my neighbour. Those hunting rifles were on the desk. He simply ridiculed these hunting rifles, and he said: If any of his soldiers or policemen were to be injured in town, he would level and raze the town to the ground. Because that is the kind of weapons that he had at his disposal. Then I turned to Malko and told him: Malko let's not raze anything to the ground. Let's leave it together, like human beings. Let's forget all of our misgivings and tensions. If there is any way. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Let's rather talk than do anything else. Let's try and see if we can live together. And then I said that we would like to see the Muslim policemen return, the ones that had been fired from the police station. And then he said to me: As long as there is no Serb policemen in Sarajevo, there is not going to be one Muslim policeman in Pale. It sounded to me like an ethnic division or an ethnic cleansing, which started with the police force and then would spread onto whatever comes next.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, if I may, Mr. Crncalo, and ask you a couple of questions. You say now that he indicated that if any of his policemen or soldiers were wounded, that he would level your settlement or your part of town. In your ICTY statement, in paragraph 21, I believe, it just says Koroman said that if any of his policemen were injured. It doesn't mention soldiers. Is your recollection that he said both policemen and soldiers, as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I hope that the Trial Chamber will understand and appreciate that I am a human being and that I can make a mistake. Maybe I have made a mistake. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is your present memory as you sit here in the courtroom about what he said?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I believe that he said what I have just told you now, as I sit today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you said in this discussion, you made reference to the fact that Muslim policemen in Pale had been dismissed. Do you know when that had begun to happen? This -- sometime prior to March 2nd or 3rd, I take it.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I know the date very well, because it happened to me as well. It was on the 15th of May. I went to work, like any other day. When I arrived at the gate, the guards simply told me that I couldn't go in. Other people came. Some were able to go in. Some weren't. Which ones were not able to go in? Only Muslims were not able to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a minute, if I can stop you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just comment, Your Honour. I'm sure Mr. Hannis will have realised himself anyway, but the question and answer, they do rather demonstrate the obvious dangers of making assumptions in the question in a leading form, because Mr. Hannis gave the witness his assumption that it was sometime prior to March the 2nd or 3rd and the answer was it was on the 15th of May. I dare say Mr. Hannis noted that discrepancy as the question and answer were given anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I don't know whether that's a danger or that it demonstrates that leading a witness in a certain direction does not always take him to that direction. But, Mr. Hannis, you certainly noted it, and I take it that you appreciate the observation made by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. I made an assumption that apparently may not be correct, and I'm going to try to clear it up now, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, we were talking about the night you were arrested and had a discussion with Mr. Koroman, and one of the topics that came up was Muslim policemen in Pale and Serbian policemen in Sarajevo. And in your answer, you said something about the 15th of May, which was when you were dismissed from work. But my question is: In March of 1992, on the 2nd or 3rd, had any Muslim policemen in Pale already been dismissed from their jobs, or did that happen later? If you know.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Policemen had already been dismissed from the police administration at Pale. I can give you their names. Suad Bajnaga [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Hudo Kadric, Meho Raketa. There was another man whose family name was Alic. I don't know his name. But I know that he hails from the local commune of Hrenovica. These people were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Koroman said -- in your statement, you indicate a particular area of Sarajevo that he talked about when he said there will be Muslim policemen here when there are Serbian policemen in that part of Sarajevo. Do you remember what part he referred to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Stari Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any significant or highly publicised event that had happened in Stari Grad about this time, in early March 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It is possible that this was the establishment of the Crisis Staff and the takeover of all political authorities in the municipality. You know what, it's very difficult for me. I'd have to think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Crncalo. I was just wondering if there was anything that was presently in your mind. That was a long time ago. I'll move on to another question. Now, after this discussion, we understand from your statement that you were eventually released from the police station and that you and your neighbour were taken home. What happened to your hunting rifle that night? Did you -- was it returned to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, it was never returned to me. It remained at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you given any kind of receipt for it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have a licence for that particular rifle?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, of course, and this rifle was registered with the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you were released and told you were free to go, what happened? Would you tell the Court how that happened. Did you and your neighbour just simply walk out and go home, or how did you get home?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: When Malko finished talking to us, he told us we could go. It was about half past 5.00 in the morning. We started walking towards the door and all of a sudden he called us to come back, and he says: You can't go on your own. I have to escort you. We looked at each other. We didn't know what was going on outside. Malko started walking in front of us. We went to the front door, and as we stepped out of the police administration building, I think I won't be mistaken when I say there were about a hundred reserve policemen around the police station. Malko was walking ahead of us amongst these people. He brought us to his car. We got into his car and he drove us to our house. On the way there, from a petrol station to the street where I lived, or maybe a hundred metres further to the left, it was all full of soldiers and policemen; that is, they were on the left-hand side. They were all facing that part of the Muslim part of Pale, and their rifles and other types of weapons were facing that area. There were machine-guns, there were people at ready with the machine-guns. And behind the machine-gunners there were ten soldiers as reinforcement. I was really surprised to see so many soldiers. I asked Malko: What is this? Malko just kept quiet. He didn't answer. Anything -- he took us to our respective houses, me and my neighbour. We were in a state of shock. We found it difficult to breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there and ask you a question. In your ICTY statement, I think you were arrested on the night of the 2nd of March. And I believe in your 1995 statement, it says the 3rd and 4th of March. Do you recall whether you were arrested on the 2nd and released the morning of the 3rd, or arrested the night of the 3rd and released the morning of the 4th? And if you don't know, that's okay too.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It may be that I was arrested on the 3rd and released on the 4th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At any rate, it was either the 2nd or the 3rd. Do you feel comfortable with that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time or shortly after of any unusual or significant event that was happening in Sarajevo about that time that may have had some connection with the presence of such large numbers of police and soldiers in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: At the time, there was a very strict control exercised by the active and reserve policemen. We were not allowed to go from one local commune to the next, and we had very little knowledge of what was going on in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In your statement, then, you talk about a public call for weapons to be surrendered. Do you recall when that happened in relation to your arrest? Was it after your arrest, and if so, approximately how long after?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: After my arrest, as far as I can remember. I can't give you the exact date; however, it was approximately 10 to 14 days later. Malko Koroman appeared on TV and invited all non-Serbs to return their long-barrelled weapons. Whatever weapons there were, were either hunting rifles or sports rifles, and they were all registered with the police. We had to surrender all of those. We had to return those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was this directed to Serbs as well?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Only non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not, when Malko Koroman made the announcement over TV, whether there was a deadline by which you had to turn in your weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. A deadline was mentioned. When we heard the announcement, on the following day, five or six people gathered, went to the police station, and spoke to Milan Simovic. They wanted an explanation of what Malko had requested the previous night from the non-Serbs. He answered: People, you have to return the weapons. There will be no more hunting. And we returned from the police station. I can't tell you what the deadline was. Maybe four days. I'm not sure. However, I'm sure that on the following day we went to the police station to ask for an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to where were the weapons to be turned in? Were you told where to turn them in?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. They said that weapons from the urban part of Pale should be brought to the police administration building. As for the local communes, a bit away from Pale, there were designated places in those local communes where the inhabitants of the local communes were supposed to bring their weapons to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you comply with this announcement to turn in weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. We had to. We were all registered with the police. Every single individual was registered with the police, and the police knew what we had, what calibre, what type of rifle. We all had hunting rifles. And there was no way for us to get away with not returning their piece or hiding from the police that they had a weapon. There was no way to hide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, the question put to you was just whether you complied. And you then started explaining for what reasons you think you could not have done otherwise. But the question just was: Did you comply? So a simple yes would have done. If Mr. Hannis would like to know whether you had any choice or any option not to comply with it, he would certainly have asked you about it. May I again direct you. It's not because it's not interesting to hear what you say, but we are under time restraints and we have to focus on those aspects that are most important for the parties and for the Chamber to hear. Mr. Hannis, we are close to 10.30. Would this be a suitable moment for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This would be fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I first ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if Rule 89(F) is applied, we usually gain some time. Could you give us an impression on how much time you would still need for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm somewhere between a third and a half of the way through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that mean that we do not save time, only four hours estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we will save time. I think we'll be under four hours, maybe three hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I think it will be under four hours, but I think it will be three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's less time saved than 89(F) would -- perhaps sometimes -- I heard a lot of details of which I asked myself what the relevance of that was. For example, if the witness says that it was from -- he knew from the First and Second World War that they were afraid. Of course you can ask him, but first of all, it creates a risk that it becomes a huge battle on who is telling the right story about the First and the Second World War, and I think the subjective fear is, at least as I understand it, is what you seek to establish, and not exactly on what recollection -- and we have had several points where I think we could have done with a little bit less details. We'll adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00. And as all parties are aware, the Chamber is really trying itself to be here back in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, when we finished, we had just been talking about Malko Koroman's call for surrender of weapons. You told us you surrendered your weapons. Do you know of any Muslims who did not surrender their weapons in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Your Honours, I want to go to paragraph 26 of your statement, Mr. Crncalo. You talk about a time when Radomir Kojic and two other men came to talk to you about leaving town. First of all, can you tell us who Radomir Kojic was?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is that 28, Your Honour? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I heard 26. I think it's 28, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No I believe it's 26 on the -- on my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The start of the campaign appears in 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The paragraph in English says ten days after my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. It's my mistake, actually. I was overlooking it was Radomir Kojic and not Mr. Koljevic. I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the question, sir? Can you tell us who Radomir Kojic was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Radomir Kojic was before the war a transporter, a hauler, and probably he was mobilised at the beginning of these events. He was probably mobilised into the reserve formation of the Serb army. I think he was in some sort of special unit as a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Radomir Kojic is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during this time, did you have any information to indicate whether he had any rank or standing in whatever unit he was in?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I saw him a couple of times while I was at Pale. He would come in front of my house with his, I suppose, duties. But he didn't have any rank insignia on him, although you could see that he was a sort of senior officer in his unit, judging by his behaviour and the conduct of the people who went with him, that he was in authority. And I saw that he had an officer's belt on him at one point, the standard type of army belt that officers wore. But he didn't carry any rank on him, rank insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of uniform did he wear? Was it a military uniform or a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: A military camouflage uniform, like the stabilising forces wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 26, you talk about an occasion about ten days after your arrest, when he and two other men, Jovan Skobo and another man named Stanar, came and talked to you. First of all, can you tell us who Jovo Skobo was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Jovan Skobo was an active-duty policeman in the Pale police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this occasion, you said they came to talk to you about leaving town. Could you tell the Judges what they said to you exactly, to the best of your memory.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They wanted to prevail upon us to have us leave the Pale municipality, and as far as I can remember, Skobo said it would be better for you to leave, to get into the buses and be transported by us somewhere else, to another area, where the Muslims are in the majority, rather than having us catch you and run off to you in the forests and woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "you," are you referring to you personally, Mr. Crncalo, or you as a group? And if so, what group?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I was present when that was what was said, and it didn't refer to me alone. It referred to the Muslim population in Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you say anything in response to this when you were told that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, yes, we did comment, but we weren't able to give any direct answer, because every time, whenever we met anybody and discussed the situation, we did try to find ways and means of remaining in our homes, in our houses, to try and find a way of continuing to live together in Pale, the way we did before all this broke out, to live a life together. We cooperated well. There were no tensions before the nationalist parties were formed. There was no tension between the nationalities before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a result of being told this by these men, did you and your Muslim neighbours contact any of the local authorities to discuss it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: It's very unpleasant to have to discuss it now, let alone when we were actually told this. We had to leave. That is to say, we had to go and see the president of the municipality. May I be allowed to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few questions first, and then if I don't cover everything, we'll give you a chance at the end. How many of you went together to see the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly a group of people, but we went several times. There were nine of us, about nine of us. Sometimes ten, sometimes eight of us, but thereabouts. The group usually numbered nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you tell the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We told him what we were told, what Skobo told us, namely, that we were being asked to move out. Why should we move away? Are we guilty of having done anything? Under what conditions, what circumstances? Why are they forcing us to leave? And he said: Who said that? Who's going to make you leave? And I said, we said: Well, a policeman turned up and told us that and the exact location where we were told to leave. And had it just been one of us who had gone to the president of the municipality to tell him that, he wouldn't have believed us, but when the nine of us went to tell him, he had to believe us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did he tell the nine of you after you reported this information to him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He told us to go to the chief of police and to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So that's Malko Koroman, as I understand. You went to see the chief of police, and did you tell him the same thing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Malko Koroman. We did tell him the same thing and asked him what we asked the mayor, the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did Mr. Koroman say to you when you told him that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He told us to go back to the president of the municipality and told us the same thing, that he couldn't guarantee our safety and security at all, as free citizens of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you tell him that you had already been to see the president of the municipality and he had referred you to Mr. Koroman?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have any other advice for you in light of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, no advice at the time. We went home after having seen the chief of police. We went back to our homes. But we discussed the situation amongst ourselves to decide what we were going to do. But we didn't find an answer, and we decided to go back and see the president of the municipality in due course, when the need arose.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple more questions about that before we go on. In your meeting with Malko Koroman, did the nine of you tell him that you had been told about leaving by one of his policemen, Jovan Skobo?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he say he would take any action with regard to Mr. Skobo or talk to him about what he had been telling you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when he said he couldn't guarantee your safety and security, did he specify what you needed to be safe and secure from?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No. He didn't specify. When we went to see the president of the municipality for the first time, and then he sent us to the chief of police, he didn't say where the danger could come from. All he said was that he couldn't guarantee our safety and security. Now, at subsequent meetings the president of the municipality and the chief of police, on one occasion Malko told us from which party he couldn't guarantee our safety and security, from what side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, based -- I think you started to say before, did you have some additional meetings and discussions with the municipality president about this problem? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, we did have a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have any additional meetings with Malko Koroman about the problem?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I gather from your statement that you didn't get any different or better answers than you had in the first meeting. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: All we were told from having talked to Malko the first time, his answer was more rigorous the second time, if anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what way? If you can explain "more rigorous."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: On one occasion we asked that somebody should be brought to the meeting from the authorities, from the peaks of power, if I can put it that way, the most highly responsible. So he didn't promise to do that, although the meeting was scheduled. We asked that it should be at the police station. But when we arrived at the police station, we were informed that the meeting would take place in a private coffee bar, the proprietor being a man named Fadil. And when we got there, Malko turned up, Roman turned up, and he sent two policemen shortly after the start of the meeting. He sent two policemen off in a car. They returned very soon, and Nikola Koljevic arrived at the meeting as well. May I be allowed to add something here, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: At the meeting, we asked Mr. Koljevic to give us guarantees that we could stay on living in Pale, stay on in our homes, and his answer to us, his response, was: It doesn't matter what you want, that you want to stay on living here, but the Serbs don't want to continue living with you here. Those were his very words. After that, Malko told us that he couldn't guarantee our safety and security, that he could no longer hold the Red Berets under his control, the Red Berets that had come from Knin. And according to him, according to what he told us, they had been put up at the Panorama Hotel and that he couldn't keep them under his control there for long. The Red Berets from Knin, that is, and some other units from other territories. He didn't tell us from which territories. And this is what he said, quite literally. He said they'd come there to do their job, to get the job done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some further details about this meeting. Do you recall approximately when this meeting took place, what month in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I'll try. I'll do my best to be as accurate as possible. The Serb government was represented at the Pale municipality, and the meeting was held after the Serb government had come to Pale, and I think it was towards the end of March, the second half of March, but I really can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, when you say after the second half of March, are you talking about when the Serb government came to Pale or are you talking about when the meeting took place, or both?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The Serb government had moved to Pale before that, prior to the meeting at which Nikola Koljevic turned up. And I can conclude this because I had the opportunity of seeing Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In person or on TV?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, as far as -- well, maybe I've got it mixed up. If I said Krajisnik -- no, I did not see Krajisnik. I saw Koljevic. That's what I meant. He came to the meeting. As for Karadzic, I saw him in front of the cultural centre when he delivered a speech there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This meeting took place before or after you were arrested on March the 2nd of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Afterwards. After my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did it also take place after the call for surrender of weapons and you had turned in your weapons?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Probably that was it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'd had at least a couple of meetings with the police chief before this meeting that Mr. Koljevic showed up at; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. We did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we know it must have taken place sometime before July 2nd of 1992, because that's when you left the municipality.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many of you -- how many Muslims were there present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: About 15 of us. I think that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were the Serb representatives? You mentioned the police chief and the president of the Municipal Assembly. Were there any others besides Mr. Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, some others did come, probably the security details, the two policemen, actually, the ones who went off to fetch him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it at this meeting where Mr. Koljevic told you what you just told the Court a short time ago, was it at this meeting that Malko Koroman talked about the Red Berets from Knin having arrived in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Koljevic was present, Mr. Koljevic was present when Malko said that he couldn't guarantee our safety because the Red Berets had arrived from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that time, whenever this meeting was, had you heard of the Red Berets from Knin before that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We never received any certain information, but, you know, rumours go around. People get to hear things. And then start passing those things on. But we didn't believe that it was true until Malko told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't believe that they were present until Malko told you? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What I was trying to ask you before, Mr. Crncalo, was: Had you or any of your Muslim neighbours heard anything about who the Red Berets from Knin were and/or anything about the kinds of activities they had been allegedly engaged in before that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, yes. We had heard about some of their activities, around Knin and Gospici, that is, in Croatia, that it was there that they did all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Without going into details about what you had heard, was the nature of what you had heard about them something that made you worried when Mr. Koroman said he might not be able to control them and they were there to do a job?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, we were all shocked when we heard the statement, and we were even more frightened as to what was going to happen to us on every subsequent night, if those Red Berets go about their business and start doing the job that Malko said they were there to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you fear that that was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, we were afraid of some kind of violence, arrests, beatings, killings, suffering, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did Malko Koroman mention this about the Red Berets being present in Pale and his being worried about not being able to control them, did he say those two things while Mr. Koljevic was at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were all in a small enough area where Mr. Koljevic could have heard it being said when it was said?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, the room was a small one. It was approximately seven or eight metres in size. It wasn't bigger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see -- did he have any reaction that you were able to see, or did he say anything about Mr. Koroman's comments about the Red Berets?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what did you and the other Muslims decide to do after having been told this by Mr. Koroman and based on what Mr. Koljevic had told you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: When we left the room, the premises, we went to my street, the street I lived on, and we discussed what we were going to do. The only way out, the only way was to save our families and that nobody should cause any kind of incident which would lead the Serbs to be nervous for any reason, to arrest somebody then and beat someone up or kill someone, as retaliation, that we should not create any incidents, just to do our best and lie low and see to the safety of our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually, while I'm on this page of his statement, page 6, I want to point to two typographical errors that appear in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I've been told by the interpreter that I'm stating this correctly. Paragraph 32, the last line, it's part of a sentence that says: After that, I never tired to go to a checkpoint. I'm told that should be I never tried to go through a checkpoint. And paragraph 35, the last line on the bottom of that page, the sentence says: These young soldiers were dresses in partial uniform. That should be "dressed" in partial uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for these clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more, Your Honour. I forgot. In paragraph 29, the second line, Red Berets is misspelled as b-a-r-e-t-s instead of b-e-r-e-t-s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was one consideration that my translator indicated that I should perhaps have the witness read a statement and have it interpreted here because there's some debate about it, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 29, the second sentence, which says: On the final visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, could you look at paragraph 29 in your ICTY statement, the one from 2001, and the second sentence, if you could read that out, and we'll have the interpreters translate it into English and see if it matches what's written here.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Shall I start on the occasion of the last visit, or final visit, latest visit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: "On the occasion of the last visit, he said that some units of the Red Berets had come to Pale and that he could not guarantee the safety of the Muslims living in that area. I was told that they were Serbs from Knin. He told us --"

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's all I needed, was that sentence. There was some question about whether it was last, final, previous visit, and whether or not it was "he said" or "he had said."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note "poslednji" can be either of those, last, final.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was our last meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was that the meeting at which Mr. Koljevic was present or was that another meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: When Koljevic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I needed to clarify on that, Your Honour. Thank you. Now, Mr. Crncalo, I want to ask you a couple of questions about checkpoints. In your statement, in paragraph 31 and 32, you talk about the existence of some checkpoints set up around the area of Pale, manned by paramilitaries and police. Would you tell the Court about the experience you had on the one occasion when you tried to go through a checkpoint.
