Who was manning the checkpoints that you passed through or attempted to pass through?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I have a piece of property a little further from Pale, and I was going there to do some work on the land, and I took -- I left from my company and came back quickly. When I reached the checkpoint, I was stopped there by some young soldiers whom I didn't know. They asked to see my ID, my papers, and as soon as they saw that my surname was Muslim, the one that was standing next to the other one looking at my documents cocked his -- directed his rifle at me and held the rifle cocked at me while I was showing them what I had in the boot of my car, what was inside the car. He asked me whether I had any weapons. I said I did not. And I said they were free to take a look. He took a look, and in the meantime, the workers were going back from work. It was 10 to 3.00 the end of the day. We all knew each other, but nobody reacted. They all sort of turned their heads away to avoid seeing what was happening to me. So I gained the impression that my colleagues from work -- that it didn't matter at all to my colleagues from work. And then I went and told what -- said what had happened to me at the -- they let me go. They let me off, past the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were the -- what kind of uniforms were these men wearing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They were wearing the typical type of uniform, winter uniforms, actually, that were worn by the army, by the military, from the communist day, from Tito's army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Tito army winter uniforms. They were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know if they were local?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I didn't recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to distinguish anything about their accent?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The one who asked to see my ID papers, I couldn't notice any accent. The other one, cocking his rifle at me, didn't say anything. He didn't utter a word. So I can't say what his accent was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you able to get to where you wanted to go that day?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. I got only halfway, and I had to return after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why did you have to return? What happened?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: As I reached the second checkpoint in front of the stambocici [phoen] tunnel, I recognised men and they recognised me, because we used to work together. The two of them approached me and asked me where I was off to. And I said: You know where I normally go. I go to my land to work. And these two men told me: Go back. You are better off not going there. And if you pass by the other checkpoint, you will be lucky. Go back home. On the way back, I was again stopped at the first checkpoint. They inspected my ID. They let me through, and after that, I could never leave home to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your two former co-workers at the second checkpoint, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were they in any kind of uniform on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. The reserve army uniforms, the winter uniforms, not the camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move on to another event, in your statement at paragraph 33 you talk about an occasion when you saw some young Muslim men being arrested down by the bus station. Can you tell us who the people were -- you described them as paramilitaries in camouflage uniforms, arresting. Do you know the ethnicity of those men who were making the arrests?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I saw three men, one of whom I recognised. The other two I didn't recognise. The other two were directly involved in that action, so to speak. They arrested people, put them in the car, and drove them off to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the person you recognised involved in this?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was my daughter's teacher, Zoran Skoba.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it Skoba?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Skobo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is he related to the Jovan Skobo who is a policeman you told us about earlier?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They are brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you also know a Rade Skobo in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I know him well. Rade Skobo is their father, and he was a medicine man. He used to treat people with herbs, and people said that he was very often successful in administering treatment to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if Rade Skobo was a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He was certainly a member of the SDS. I don't know whether he held any other positions. I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, one of the previous questions has not been fully answered, and I'd like to solicit an answer from the witness. You told us, Mr. Crncalo, that the three paramilitaries in camouflage uniforms who made the arrest, that you knew one of them, but the question was put to you what their ethnicity was. Could you tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have been asked several times -- let me first ask you: The other two were unknown to you, as far as I understand. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you know that the other two unknown to you were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the Republika Srpska army did not have any other ethnic groups, so it could not have been any other ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the paramilitaries were members of the -- were part of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then a similar question in respect of the three policemen who came to arrest you. You testified that you didn't know them, but you also testified that they were Serbs. How did you know that they were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but how did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A minute ago I was talking about mobilisation, which took place while I still worked, while I still could go to work. No Muslim was ever called. No Muslim ever received call-up papers. Just the Serbs did. Nobody in Pale could be either a policeman or a soldier but the Serbs, because at that time all the Muslims had already been dismissed from work. It could only be Serbs. Only Serbs could be members of either the reserve army or the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Zoran Skobo, who you saw on this date at the bus station, was he wearing any kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any insignia on that or rank?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I didn't see any. Even if there had been any, it would have been very hard for me to notice them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Mr. Crncalo, I want to ask you about paragraph 34. You talk about sometime in April or May of 1992, your telephone service was cut off. Do you know if the telephone service was cut off for all citizens in Pale municipality, or only a certain group?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Only a certain group of population was cut off. There were women who went to ask the Serb women to give them access to the telephone so that they could inquire about their relatives in Sarajevo. That is how I know that only non-Serbs had their telephone lines cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have your own telephone service cut off?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness a document now, the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be number, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P272.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is an order with a list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is an order with a list of names, and the ERN is 0208-9424.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, I suppose I should ask you first: Do you read Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 7th of May, 1992, which purports to be an order from the Crisis Staff of Pale, about disconnecting certain phone lines. Would you look at the names on that list and tell me if you recognise, first of all, the person listed at number 12.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I recognise that name. We were arrested together on that night, on the 3rd or the 4th of March. I was arrested first, and then half an hour later he was brought in. His name is Munib Kadric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us what the ethnicity of the 15 people on that list would be, based on their names?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, were you given any prior warning or indication that your telephone service was going to be cut off?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You can set that document aside now. I'm finished with it. Mr. Crncalo, you state in your ICTY statement, in paragraph 35, that in May and June of 1992, you noticed a bigger concentration of military equipment and military presence. Can you tell the Judges what you began to notice about that time in terms of the increased military presence? What kinds of soldiers, and how many were you seeing that you had not seen previously?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Next to the Famos factory, there is a place where you could store wheat. Big lorries would pass by, and as they were passing by, you could tell that they were loaded. I suppose that there was grain in the lorries. And they were escorted by armoured vehicles. That was at the beginning. Later on, instead of those lorries, you could see an occasional lorry, but also you could see military vehicles. They didn't all go towards silo, but towards the Jahorinski Potok barracks. It lasted for days, and later on there were buses loaded with troops. And the most difficult thing for us to see were half-dressed young men. They were bare-chested. Mind you, it was hot. They had armbands. They had bands around their heads. They had knives on both of their flanks. They had rifles, pistols, hand grenades. They drove by in convertibles. They acted in a very arrogant way and they instilled fear in us. Every now and then, you could see them in Pale, in all the streets. On two occasions, they came up to my house and they inquired about my neighbour's lorry. The first time they appeared, I was stunned with fear. I didn't know what would happen. They asked me who the car belonged to. I couldn't speak. My neighbour appeared and nodded towards me, and I told him: They're inquiring about the car. He said the car was his. And they said: Okay. We'll come back later to inspect the car. Maybe we'll need it. They behaved as if there was no control over them, as if there was nobody who could prevent them from doing anything that they wanted to do. At least, that's the way they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. These two that came to your house in particular, I think you said it was two, did you have a conversation with them? And if so, were you able to tell anything from their accent where they were from?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They were not locals. They had a slightly different accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've described this group of military types that don't sound like a regular army. You say they were bare-chested and they had two knives and they were wearing headbands, et cetera. How many of these kind of military men or young men did you see in Pale municipality during this time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Truth be told, I could give you my estimate, but I can't give you their exact number. There were hundreds of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In addition to those, were there what appeared to be more regular army-type soldiers stationed in Pale or present in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Shall I compare the ones that were only partially dressed and the regular troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. If you can give me an estimate based on that comparison.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There were more regular troops than those that were poorly dressed or half dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Crncalo, I want to ask you a question, and first of all, I'll ask you a yes-or-no question. Based on what you saw of these, we'll say, non-regular soldiers, and which you described as paramilitary in your statement, based on what you saw of them, and given the size of the town of Pale that you told us about and the way they were behaving, do you have an opinion - yes or no - about whether those troops could have gone unnoticed by anybody living and working in Pale at that time? Yes or no. Do you have an opinion?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They could not go unnoticed. All day long they were moving around Pale in their cars. They would stop by the bus station. They would pop in a coffee bar, have something to drink. Then they would go back to their cars and continue driving up and down. The town of Pale was full of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier, I think, that there was a time prior to May and June when the Republika Srpska government had relocated its headquarters to Pale. Do you know where in Pale their headquarters were located?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, the TV station was also close to the culture centre, and on one occasion I saw Mr. Karadzic delivering a speech there. So judging by all that, I would say that they were in the culture centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever learn that they were in another location later on, or was that the only place you believed or were aware that they were located?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I have just remembered a detail with regard to the culture centre, and I can now say with more certainty that the government must have been in the culture centre, because there were six soldiers standing guard in front of the culture centre. So judging by that, it is certain that it was in the culture centre. Very soon, it was relocated to another place close to the railway station. The name of the place is Koran. That's where a flyover is now. This is where the government premises used to be in Pale municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, can you tell where the cultural centre was located in Pale in relation to the police station? Was it nearby? How far, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Close to the police station. I won't be wrong if I say that the distance was 350 to 400 metres. And it was the building adjacent to the Orthodox Church.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the second area you told us about, Koran, is that in Pale, the town? How far is that from the cultural centre and the police station that you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It is in Pale, in the town of Pale. The local commune is also called Koran. And the distance between the cultural centre and the police and Koran is about a kilometre, maybe not even that. But let's say that it is about a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to ask you about something described in paragraph 36 of your statement. You talk about an occasion in May 1992 when you saw three truckloads of men arriving in town and you say that these were some Muslim men from Bratunac. How did you get the information that these were Muslim men from Bratunac? What was your source?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I heard it on the spot. There were people standing next to those trucks, saying: Balijas had been captured in Bratunac and brought here to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you actually see the men that were on the truck?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them on the truck. Some had scars on their bodies. Not all of them, but some did. And I would say that they had been gathered from their stables and fields, because it was the time of spring sowing. I would say that they were just gathered from wherever they were at the time. I would never say that they were members of any army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of clothing were they dressed in?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Civilian clothes, rubber boots, overalls, working clothes. Some wore jumpers. Some had their boots soiled with excrement, with manure. That's why I know that they had been gathered from their stables, from their workplaces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your earlier answer about what you saw, you said some had -- it's translated in English as: Some had scars on their bodies. Scar to me indicates the healing of an old wound. Are you talking about old wounds or fresher wounds?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: You could see drying blood on their faces, which means that those were fresh wounds. Those were not lethal wounds, but just wounds that people sustained from having been beaten by something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: What time day or night was this that you saw these trucks arrive? If you remember.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It was during the day, around noon, or sometime between noon and 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what part of town were you in, or were these trucks in when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Close to the police station, towards the cultural centre. That's where the lorries were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you describe the president of the municipality coming out and saying something. Were you actually close enough to hear him have that discussion about what to be done with these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He came and he was embarrassed. He didn't know what to do with these people. His comment was: Why did you bring them here? I don't have anywhere to put them. Take them back from where you brought them. I don't know his name, his first name. I know that his family name was Starcevic and this was his comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, may I again ask you to carefully listen to the question, because what that person said appears in your statement. But the specific question put to you was whether you were close enough to hear the conversation of this person with the men on the truck. So that's what Mr. Hannis wanted to know from you. We know already from your statement what he said. Could you please answer that question now, whether you were close enough, perhaps at what distance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't -- he wasn't talking to the people that were brought into the truck. He didn't say anything to them at all. I was quite close, so I could hear or not hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And to whom did he then speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the drivers that drove them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you said you were close enough. At what distance, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About ten metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you able to see who the drivers of these trucks were and whether or not they were wearing any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No. They had that -- the uniforms of the regular army formations, but no insignia that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where was the place that Mr. Starcevic told the drivers to take these people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I understood it that they were taking them from where they had come, to Bratunac, that is, and I heard the locals say that they had brought in the balijas from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe you misunderstood. Where did Mr. Starcevic say the drivers should put those prisoners in Pale? In your statement, you say the cinema, but can you tell me where the cinema is in relation to the police station, for example? How close is that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He said that they should take them back to where they came from. But yes, they did take them to the cinema hall, and the cinema hall is right by the police station. How far? Well, about 20 metres in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, Mr. Crncalo, I want to ask you about the occasion when you went to work and were told that you should go home and that you weren't going to have to come in to work any more. The first thing I want to ask you: In your ICTY statement, you referred to that as happening on May 15th of 1992, which by my calendar appears to have been on a Friday. And I believe in your 1995 statement to the High Court in Sarajevo, you mention the date of the 27th of May, which again by my calendar I think is a Wednesday. As you sit here today now, do you know whether it was the 15th of May or the 27th of May?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I think it was on the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in helping you place it in time, do you know if that occurred, the event at work, when you were told to go home, did that occur before or after you had seen these men from Bratunac arrive on the trucks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall if it occurred before or after you and your -- some of your neighbours had had the meeting with -- which Mr. Koljevic attended? Before or after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It was before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, next I want to go to paragraph 40 in your ICTY statement, where you talk about in late June and early July, convoys to remove Muslims being organised. How were you and your neighbours, your Muslim neighbours, informed about this fact, that there were going to be convoys to take Muslims out of Pale? Did you see it on TV? Did someone come and tell you? How did you find out?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: It was on television. Or rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat whether it was or was not on television. Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They said that a part of Pale -- there would be written instructions and one location would be pinpointed for one day and then for the next day and that everybody would be informed when written information would be sent as to which part of Pale should withdraw, on what day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, was this on television that you heard this or was that by any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could he repeat it again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The interpreters are having some difficulties in understanding exactly or hearing exactly what you say. Could you please perhaps -- was it on television you heard it? Could you please answer by yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, it wasn't on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then where or when did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Kojic came and Skobo came, and launched their propaganda to the effect that we should move out, that was the first piece of information that we were required to move out. But we didn't believe it, and not to waste your time, the last time there was a notice printed up on a visible place in town, a written notice, saying that one street would have to move away, and then another. People didn't comment. They just came and gathered at one particular location. They boarded buses and were taken away. So that's what happened. The written notice, it started around the veterinary station Slavisa Vajnar Cice was the street, part of that street near the veterinary station. They rounded up all the people and they were taken off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you found a kind of a schedule on that piece of paper who would have to go, when, to the buses; is that correct? I see you're nodding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're now also saying yes. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I understand, Mr. Crncalo: Then even though it had been talked about before, the first sort of official, in black and white, notice that this was actually happening was an announcement printed on a piece of paper and posted somewhere in the neighbourhood where people were going to have to be leaving from; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the announcement have any information on it about who this schedule for departure was coming from? Was there any official reference to an agency or a body that was setting this up? Or did it just have a schedule: 9.00, be at this location?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No political party or structure, the municipality or the police, took over responsibility for that. There was just this information saying that we had to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you go to talk to anybody about that to ask whose idea was this, and did you really have to go?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, yes. A number of times we did talk to the chief of police and the chief of the municipality when the first convoy left towards Sarajevo, a day or two afterwards we went to see the municipality president to ask him again what had happened to those people, why did those people have to leave, what have you done to the people? And he said: They must have infringed upon the law in some way, done something unlawful. But then we said: But they'll say the same about us. They'll say that we did something against the law and that we would have to move out, whereas we had done nothing yet. Whereas if we get on the bus, that would automatically mean that we had done something wrong, something illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did he say when you told him about that and pointed that out to him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: He didn't say anything. He made no comment. When we said that we would probably be -- that it would probably be said that we had done something against the law if we had boarded the buses and were taken off somewhere, that the same would happen to us. We didn't know at which destination, but he just kept quiet. He didn't have an answer to give us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So do you know whose decision it was that the Muslims were going to have to get on buses and leave Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We asked for the possibility of getting a reply from the president of the municipality and the chief of police, whereas they kept sending us from one to the other. But neither of them gave us an answer. And then we concluded that most probably the decision was taken by the SDS Crisis Staff, that that should be done, that what happened should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you said before you had a home in Pale. Did you own your property? Did you own your house in Pale at that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was the owner of my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have to make some arrangement about that before you left Pale? What became of your property?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: A woman came by and said she wanted to move into my house, and she gave me the address of her own house in Sarajevo. And she said that I was to go with her to the municipality building to sign a contract of some kind. And I had no choice. I had to go to the municipality. I was a little surprised by it all, because it was all typed up. There were forms that were already typed out, standard forms, and they introduced our data, mine and hers. And the agreement was that I should hand over the keys and leave my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was this woman who came to your house, and what was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Her name was Dragica Subotic. She was a Serb and she had two sons, Miro and Zoran. I saw Miro. I didn't see Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why was your house the one that she picked? If you know.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you want to exchange your house for her property?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I mentioned on one occasion that at my place of work, in our company, they asked me when I was going to leave my house, and I said that I cannot, neither do I wish to leave my house, for as long as I'm alive. But when I saw what was happening, I decided to save my life and the lives of my family members rather than save my house, so I had to relinquish it and hand it over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When she came and told you that you had to go somewhere and sign some papers, did she say whether you had a choice about whether to sign or not?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The police on one occasion said: If anybody refused to do so, they had to go to the police station and leave the keys there, the keys to their houses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did there come a time about then when a notice appeared in your neighbourhood saying that you and your neighbours were going to have to get on a bus, a convoy, and leave?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you've told us before you left on the 2nd of July, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know how many convoys had already left Pale with Muslims before the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Two convoys, and I was in the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many people left in those first two convoys? If you can give us an approximate number.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The buses were packed full. There were seven buses in the first convoy and six in the second. In my particular convoy, there were five. I don't know about the other two convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were these standard, full sized buses, and approximately how many people were in each one, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The buses were the intercity type of bus line, which takes about a hundred people. The number of seats plus the number of standing places. So certainly, 90, and probably more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about your personal property -- well, first of all, did you own a car in addition to your house?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a car.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What became of it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I had to leave my car behind too, and the keys to the car, and my driving permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how much personal property were you allowed to take out with you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: What we could carry. That's what we were allowed to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, after these 18 buses of Muslims were driven out of Pale, do you know, were there any Muslims remaining in Pale after your convoy left?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Some people did stay. Two convoys from the urban part of Pale. And then they went to the local communes and the villages, to evacuate those people and to transport them to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Muslims who stayed behind and did not go out on any of these convoys?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: About 12, perhaps a little more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you consulting your statement, Mr. Crncalo? I saw you looking down, so I just wondered whether you -- yes, you have written notes there or ... Mr. Hannis, it was unclear, to me at least, what source was consulted by the witness, and could you please -- of course, I can imagine -- yes, could you please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, the Judge was just asking you if you were looking at something in relation to the last question. Can you tell him what that is that you have in your hand that you were referring to, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I just counted the people who stayed behind in Pale, those who did not leave in the convoys, who stayed on to live in their own houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can I ask you what that piece of paper is that you were looking at just then. What is that? Where does that come from? Who wrote that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when did you write that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I wrote it a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for what purpose did you write that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, before I gave a statement to The Hague investigators, using the same piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, then, that this is an aide memoire that is consulted. I have no further questions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. Your Honour, perhaps just out of -- Ms. Cmeric suggests for precaution's sake perhaps the witness should take his headphones off for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I then would prefer that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm nearly finished, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, Mr. Stewart, nearly finished means a couple of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five minutes. I would now continue, then have a break. But before we have the break and we ask the witness to leave the courtroom and whatever has to be said could be said at that moment. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you looking at that note just now to count up the number of names of people you knew who remained behind?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And having done that, does that refresh your recollection about approximately how many people were left behind, that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I just wanted to check whether I was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you? And if so, what was that number?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I said 12, and I can give you this list to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. That's all right. And did you later learn what happened to those 12 people who remained behind in Pale? What was their fate during the war? I just need a short answer. I don't need specifics about each one.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: They were all killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Lastly, Your Honour, I would like to show the witness one more exhibit. The English ERN is 0304-6729. The B/C/S is 0207-2618.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P273 for the original B/C/S and P273.1 for the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, while that's on the way, I want to ask you: Before you left Pale, did you see any Red Berets in Pale, and if so, where were they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: When we got into the buses and started out, near the Panorama Hotel, behind a privately owned house, I saw some soldiers wearing red berets. Two of them -- that's where I saw the Red Berets, as far as Pale goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that was on the day that you left, on the 2nd of July?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: 2nd of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to ask you about the document you've been handed, and if my learned friend will accept this, what I propose to do is just read one paragraph and ask him for a comment. Mr. Crncalo, this is a document dated the 19th of July, from the -- purportedly from the Serbian Republic Presidency, and the first paragraph says: It's directed to several municipalities, including Pale municipality, and it says in the first paragraph: In close cooperation with public security stations, you are kindly requested to make an inventory of all housing facilities, summer cottages, houses, and flats, in your municipality that are vacant following the voluntary departure of Muslims. Mr. Crncalo, my question to you is: Was your departure from Pale voluntary?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, nor would I ever have done that voluntarily, to leave my house and leave all my property behind, everything that I had accrued during my years of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I was forced to. I was forced to sign that contract on the exchange and to leave my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those are all the questions I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Crncalo, we'll have a break now, and after the break you'll be examined by counsel for the Defence. Madam Usher, could you escort the witness out of the courtroom. And Mr. Stewart, I'll then give you an opportunity to just make ... If you could ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart, or Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we need to address the issue of the piece of paper he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was wondering. I couldn't see what happened, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's actually gone out in the witness's pocket, Your Honour, which is -- which is maybe -- probably what Your Honour noticed. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that and I asked myself whether I had to call him back and to see whether I had to instruct him to keep it or not. I take it that it's in his pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd rather come to the conclusion that the witness came back and announced that he had destroyed the piece of paper or lost it over the few minutes out of court that that would raise questions so I decided not to mention that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I wondered whether we would -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber takes no further action in respect of the paper at this moment, the piece of paper. Was there anything else you'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, the question of the paper leaving the court came after I stood up to say something about it, so I clearly must have had another point in mind, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the right pocket, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That seems to be a detail, Your Honour. The -- Your Honour, the piece of paper, well, first of all, may I just say as a matter of general practice and it's just for the future, it's not a big deal as far as the past is concerned, it would be a good idea, we suggest, if perhaps the usher could be instructed just to ensure as a matter of housekeeping that any witness giving evidence only has on the table in front of that witness the specific material that counsel are inviting or the Tribunal are inviting the witness to look at. We've had this once or twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd rather ask the parties to keep an eye on that, because Madam Usher is at approximately the same distance as I usually am, and of course if she sees there are documents not handed out to the witness she could inform the registrar, or could then inform me and we could ask for this. But if either of the parties sees that the witness is consulting documents that are unknown to the Chamber or to the other party, that my intention is drawn to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, absolutely, entirely. We -- we -- I wasn't for one moment -- I don't suppose Mr. Hannis would either -- I wasn't for one moment attempting to shuffle off that responsibility. We do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We do that anyway, Your Honour. It's just that the usher has frequent opportunities in the course of the case to be very close to the desk which we don't have. That's all. So, as a supplement to our alertness that would be helpful. But the more substantial point, Your Honour, is that I asked to see and have the opportunity of taking a copy of that note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask the witness to, after we have resumed, the first thing I'll ask him to -- ask him first of all whether he has any objection to show it to you. And then we'll see what happens. Yes, if he voluntarily does --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. We'll take it step by step in the way that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I suggest. So we'll do that after the break. We'll have a break for 20 minutes, we'll resume at 10 minutes to 1.00. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, do you remember that we briefly discussed the small memo you had. Do you hear me? Yes. We discussed the small memo you consulted. I even noticed that you offered to Mr. Hannis to look at it. Would you mind if Defence counsel would have a look at that piece of paper you consulted? Yes? Well, if you -- if you would ask Madam Usher to give it, then, to Mr. Stewart. It will be returned to you anyhow, but perhaps it might be asked that a copy would be made. But -- so it's open to everyone what piece of paper you consulted at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. We'd like to make a copy. The only question is what's the most practically convenient. We needn't have a long debate about it. We can arrange to have a copy made straight away or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the proper way of doing it is asking the registrar. Madam Usher if you'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's preferable for us, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will remain in the hands of the Chamber, or at least of the usher. We'll make a copy of it and the original will be returned to you for the time being, unless there would be any reason why the original would be needed. But it at least gives you an opportunity to consult the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That seems unlikely. We've had a glance. It seems unlikely. It looks as if a photocopy is going to be perfectly adequate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hope the usher is aware that it's a document with two sides written on. Yes. Then, Mr. Crncalo, you'll now be examined by Mr. Stewart, who is counsel for the Defence. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, first of all, mobilisation, which came up in the course of your evidence this morning, the position was this, wasn't it, that Muslims in your area were, in fact, officially called up to join the army, but that the Muslim leaders directed them not to go. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a time frame for that? Because he was talking about, I think, May of 1992, and there were more than one mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please specify or -- Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I misspoke. I think I said May, and I meant Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least the witness answered this morning questions about whether or not actually being called for mobilisation, and I take it that we're referring to that answer, Mr. Stewart, or is it broader?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. I was referring to his -- as I introduced my question to his specific evidence given this morning. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, Mr. Crncalo, the question is whether it was not the case when you talked this morning about mobilisation that Muslims actually were mobilised but were advised not to respond to any call for mobilisation. Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not mention any advice given about mobilisation. The only people that were called up were Serbs. Muslims were never invited to join the army, either orally or in a written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, let's get it absolutely clear, then, Mr. Crncalo. First of all, are you aware that in the course of, I think it was late 1991, but certainly at the beginning of 1992, that in at least some parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a call-up to join the army, a call-up of Serbs, Muslims, possibly others, but certainly a call-up that included both Serbs and Muslims? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I am. I'm aware of that. I heard it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did I stop your answer?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. It was suggested by the political structures from Sarajevo that such a mobilisation call should not be responded to. In 1992, Pale and Sarajevo were two totally separate places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Two separate -- well, they're two separate places. We know that. Physically. But in what sense do you mean that Sarajevo and Pale were two separate places?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Whatever suggestions came from Sarajevo, they couldn't do anything to either help us or not help us. I'm talking about the population. I am talking about what was going on in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, in the first few months - January, February, March - of 1992, Sarajevo was in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Pale was, and still is, in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You were aware, you say, from the television, you were aware that there was in many parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina a call-up. This was the JNA, a call-up of men, including both Muslims and Serbs. We're agreed on that much so far, are we?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In 1992, that is, from the beginning of 1992, if I may be allowed to explain the situation to you that prevailed in Pale at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we just confirm your agreement so far to what I've just put to you, and then that gives us a starting point. Do you need it to be repeated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, I don't need this to be repeated. I've heard you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I was going to ask that it be supplemented with a specific time frame, because as I understand it, there were two or three different call-ups at different times in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the time frame that I indicated in my question was January, February, March 1992. We believe that the answers this morning in relation to mobilisation related to within that period, January 1992. So I'm content for the moment to proceed on the basis of January 1992, so that -- I'll put it this way to you: In January 1992, you were aware, were you, from the television, that there was in many parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina a call-up to the JNA of men, including indiscriminately Muslims and Serbs? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you say, then, that although that occurred in many parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that in Pale, that call-up did not include Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In Pale, written call-ups for mobilisation were only sent to the Serbs, to the people of Serb origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: While I still worked, only the Serbs were mobilised. None of the Muslims ever received call-up papers, nor did they join the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So on the first point about whether they received call-up papers, you say that from your discussions with your work colleagues, you heard enough on this topic to reach a reliable conclusion that although Serbs were receiving call-up papers, Muslims were not? That's what you say, is it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. What I've just said. I can add something to that if you will allow me, if I have time to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it in answer to my question, what you wish to add?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, please do, then.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: If anybody had received call-up papers, they would have had to respond. There was no other way out of that. Because the military police was still in place, the way if existed before the war. So if anybody had failed to respond to the call-up, they would have had to be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Crncalo, that in at least some other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Muslims, on quite a significant scale, did not respond to their call-up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know about other parts of Bosnia. I know what was going on in Pale. I don't know what was going on in other parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware of any sort of direction or advice coming from Muslim leaders in relation to any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina that Muslims should not respond to their call-up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Like I've just said a while ago, I heard such comments on TV. However, an ordinary person, an ordinary man from the street, should they have received call-up papers, they had to respond. If they had failed to do that, they would have been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you about a different topic, then. Let me ask you about what you've described in your evidence concerning the 6th of May, 1991. Now, the 6th of May is or it certainly was in that year a traditional Serb holiday. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in your statement, this is paragraph 11 of your -- what I'll call your main statement, given to this Tribunal on the 8th of June, 2001, you've said that Seselj had re-established the Chetniks on the Romanija mountain at Novakova Pecina. Now, in what sense and to what degree do you say that Mr. Seselj re-established the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I have just said that it is part of the Hajduk tradition, this Novak's cave on Mount Romanija, and although the Chetnik movement was abolished, Seselj wanted to re-establish it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But what do you say actually happened that constitutes a re-establishment of the Chetniks on or around the 6th of May, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: If you were to live in that part of Bosnia where Pale is, then you would understand things more clearly. You would know exactly what I meant. I meant what I said. I said what happened. Seselj's supporters went up there. I don't know what they did in the cave or around the cave. However, I heard later on from the Serbs, the inhabitants of these areas, that on the way back, Seselj had fallen from his horse and that he had hurt his head, probably because he was drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we won't worry about the last point, Mr. Crncalo. May I simply, for future reference on these questions, may I in a sense point out to you the obvious, that I do not live and never have lived in that part of Bosnia or indeed in any other parts of Bosnia, so my understanding is not the point. I ask you questions so that the Tribunal and everybody else can understand what you say about these matters. So please make no assumptions about any knowledge on my part and assume that I have none. The -- so you still haven't answered my question, which is: What do you say actually happened on or around the 6th of May, 1991, that could sensibly be described as a re-establishment of the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: There was a rally, a meeting, which served to reinforce the Radical Party, Seselj's Radical Party. I don't know what Seselj intended to do with that rally, but I believe that it served to increase the number of his party members.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The truth is, Mr. Crncalo, that there was, as there always is every year, there was a public celebration held at Novak's cave. On that particular occasion, whether or not he had ever been there before or since, on that particular occasion Mr. Seselj was there, maybe he fell down drunk and hurt his head, who knows, but he was there. But there really is no more to it than that, as far as this Chetnik issue, is there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: We expected that something bad would happen, bad for us. But thank God, it didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, subsequently you were, as you described, you were reassured by Serbs, weren't you, that there wasn't actually anything seriously to worry about at that time in early summer and in the summer of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Nothing significant happened after that. Seselj came. He held his rally. Where he went next, I don't know. In any case, after his arrival and departure, there were no significant incidents. However, this event instilled some fear into us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. You've said that. And then the -- and after a while, you started some sort of guard activities and then after a while you dropped them, didn't you, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you describe in your statement, and this is paragraph 14, you say: During this time, and that's 1991, the second half of 1991 you're talking about, you said that -- well, in the previous paragraph, 13, you said: If the Chetniks and Serbs held meetings, they were held outside the city centre. Now, you don't know whether the Chetniks held any meetings at all in the second half of 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that. Seselj's Radical Party and its supporters that are being mentioned now, as far as I know, were located at Novak's cave. All the other rallies and demonstrations from 1991 to the beginning of the war itself would be often held in the centre of Pale and they were shouting: We won't yield Kosovo. They were carrying a coffin containing the bones of Tsar Lazar. That's at least what I was told. All those who attended the rally said that were Tsar Lazar's bones in it. And they were inviting people to join their rallies and demonstrations. They would go through the very centre of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Respectful suggestion. You started saying I don't know how to answer that question. May I make a respectful suggestion, Mr. Crncalo, that the first step would be to listen to my question and then try directly to answer the question that I ask you. And the question was I put to you: You don't know whether the Chetniks held any meetings at all in the second half of 1991, do you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when -- after the 6th of May, 1991, then, and we've -- I don't want to pursue the cave any more- but after the 6th of May, 1991, when do you say was the next meeting that took place of the Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: On the 6th of May again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Try to be specific there, Mr. Crncalo. Forget the 6th of May. Let's move on from the 6th of May. When do you say that the next meeting after the 6th of May of the Chetniks was held?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact you don't know if any further meeting was held, do you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Between the 6th of May and the next year 6th of May, I don't know whether there were any meetings of the Radical Party and these radical people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when you say the Radical Party, you mean Chetniks, do you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In paragraph 14 of your statement, then, you -- during this time, and it was the same period that you're talking about in that statement, that's apparent, "during this time, the members of the Chetnik organisation started wearing uniforms and special Chetnik hats." Now, the position was this, Mr. Crncalo, wasn't it, that there was no established Chetnik organisation in Pale between May 1991 and the end of 1991, was there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: What I said about the 6th of May and Seselj is what I know. I can't provide you with any documentation and I can't tell you anything precisely about the establishment of that party or give you any dates. I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for documentation, Mr. Crncalo. When I want to ask you for documentation, I will make that very clear. What I'm putting to you is that from -- after the 6th of May, 1991, and in fact I'll take it right through to April 1992, there was no Chetnik organisation in Pale. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, can you, then, describe the scale, size, and nature of the Chetnik organisation in Pale during that period?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: All I can say is that I saw at the petrol station two men wearing the kind of uniform that I described today and that the people I knew, the Serb people I knew, when we were waiting in line to tank up, they said that: There, you have Sulejman what the Chetniks look like. You can have a look there and I described what they looked like and what uniforms they wore this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in your statement when you say that during this time the members of the Chetnik organisation started wearing uniforms and special Chetnik hats, it is only those two men at the petrol station that you actually observed yourself wearing Chetnik uniforms and hats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you also said in your statement, same paragraph, paragraph 14: "I believed these Chetniks had weapons because many Chetniks went to fight at Pakrac, Croatia, and they kept their weapons when they returned to the Pale area." When you say many Chetniks went to fight at Pakrac, Croatia, you mean, do you, many Chetniks from Pale?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many -- do you know the answer -- I'll rephrase. As far as you know, how many men from Pale went to fight in Croatia? And the timescale is the war in Croatia, which, broadly speaking, went right through to the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Upon returning from those parts of Croatia, the state of Croatia now, they were proud in their behaviour and they talked proudly and said that they were the men of Vukovar, the Vukovarci, or that they had returned from Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, the question was: How many men from Pale went to fight in Croatia? Your answer was about how those returning from Croatia behaved. You explained: Proudly. But if Mr. Stewart would like to know how they behaved, he'll ask you. So could you tell us how many men, approximately, from Pale went to Croatia to fight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have the possibility of knowing the number of people who went there, so I can't give you a precise answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "many." Could you give an indication of what you understood when you said "many"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the only thing that I could say is that from time to time, if I were to add everybody up, I would say about 50. So that would be my rough assessment, as far as I know. But as to what I don't know, I'm sure that I know very little in comparison to the whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us, that you knew about approximately 50, but it might have been more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Crncalo, Ms. Cmeric suggests that included in that answer was a reference by the witness to his having heard that the way it's come across on the transcript is "the only thing I could say is that from time to time if I were to add everybody up, I would say about 50." That's expressed in unqualified terms in translation. But Ms. Cmeric suggests that the witness said that he heard. Is that -- perhaps I can ask it this way, Your Honour. Is this -- this figure of 50 or about 50 that you put forward, is that based on what you were told by other people or heard from other people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, when I was in the company of people, of those people, coming back from those battlefields, when they were talking amongst themselves that they were in those two parts of the battleground, listening to them, that's what I concluded. I didn't hear it from them, but listening to them talk, that's what I concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were they people at work or people that you met in a cafe, or what?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: At work, and I don't frequent cafes much. So at work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So people from your work, is this what you say, people from your work went to fight in Croatia and returned from fighting in Croatia? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In that case, presumably, Mr. Crncalo, if it's people from your work, you do have a pretty firm idea of how many were involved, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Where I worked in the factory, there were 3.000 people, and I can't know each of those employees, all those workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the moment, I'm suggesting to you that even among 3.000 employees, you would have had a pretty firm idea of how many of those 3.000 went to Croatia and returned from fighting in Croatia. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have a precise picture of it all, but that's what was common knowledge, at least on the shift I was working, and we worked in three shifts. In the other two shifts, there were quite a number of people whom I didn't know, so I don't know whether they went or not. But the people working in my own shift, they would say, and judging on what the other -- the men in the other two shifts say -- but as I say, I didn't know anybody personally, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many men were on your shift?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: About 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how many -- was it the same people constantly, was it, broadly speaking, the same 90, not every day, but roughly speaking, it was the same group of men continuing on the same shift, month in, month out, was it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. But you know how it was. There would be new workers coming in. Some would retire, other young workers would come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course there would be changes. That's understood. How many men from your shift went to fight in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Three.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: One was Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First name?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So one was Jovic. Another one?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Gajovic, not Jovic. Gajovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. That's one. Another one?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Micic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the third?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Todorovic was this one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did they all return?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And how long were they away? Maybe not all the same period, but how long were they away?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Not long. About 15 days, one month, and then they came back. But they didn't go to work afterwards. They carried on with their military activities in the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And units of what? What were they -- in what units were they fighting?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In those military units. I don't know the names of those units they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They weren't Chetniks, were they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what structures they were in. I really can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But was there anything about your three work colleagues to indicate that they were what you regarded as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, we thought along these lines: First of all, the people that were prone to those radical moves, that they were the first to join the fighting. Now, whether they were those or not, it was our understanding that they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So let me get this straight. Well, I'll put the question another way. Apart from the fact that they -- the simple fact that they went to Croatia to fight, do you know anything else about those work colleagues of yours which indicated that they were what you regarded as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I don't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of anybody called Jovo Civkovic -- Svicovic might be a better attempt, Svicovic, Jovo Svicovic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, the surname doesn't ring a bell as being a surname that we had in the Pale municipality. Possibly he came from other parts and settled there, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you don't know anybody of that name. That's what you're saying; right? You don't, and never did?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: No, I don't. Nobody with that surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- because the -- the true position is this, isn't it, Mr. Crncalo, that only a very tiny number of men went to Croatia at all to fight from Pale, much less than the 50 that you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: As I said, the 50, that is my assessment. And I think I'm right in saying that. Now, the fact that I cannot give you the name and surname of each individual person, what can I do?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you could be wrong about it. It could be, from what you know, it could be that significantly fewer than 50 men ever went to fight in Croatia from Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I'll stand by what I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, is it -- is it correct that shortly before the start of the war, two of your cousins were arrested?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And they were arrested because they had been trading in illegal weapons; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The sale of weapons? I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did they live in the same village as you? Radacici, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Yes. Radacici. But I didn't live there. I haven't lived there since 1969. I hadn't lived there since then. I was born there. That's true. But I never actually lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Did your cousins live in Radacici, then, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: I did have some family there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's be clear. We're talking about these two cousins who were arrested. Could you just give us their names, please, so there's no ambiguity about it. The names, please, of the two cousins of yours who were arrested.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Crncalo Nisad and Crncalo Emir, they were arrested at the bus station in Pale and they were under custody for about three hours and then released.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were they -- did they live in Radacici, both of them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: In Pale, not in Radacici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They were brothers, were they, those two cousins?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: The two of them were brothers. The Crncalo brothers, Nisad and Emir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's correct that their arrest was in connection with trading in illegal weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Objection. I think it's been asked and answered that he didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, he has been asked. The answer to the question, I'll just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, he answered it in the sense he said I don't know about that, but occasionally, Your Honour, witnesses give answers which justify a little pressing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- Mr. Crncalo, do you know what your cousins were arrested for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This morning, I mentioned the act of arrest of the people in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you know for what your cousins were arrested.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What were they arrested for? They were suspected of something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were picked up off the street, 19 of them, including my two cousins, 19 young men. I know about that. As for the others ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then were they suspected of anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they weren't suspected of anything. Because they were Muslims, that's why they were taken to prison, and we intervened, we went to the police station, and they were released, two and a half or three hours later. And all 19 of them were released, in actual fact, and they were never arrested again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Crncalo, that's not true. Your two arrested cousins were taken to the central prison in Sarajevo, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN CRNCALO
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to hear the names of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have other cousins who were arrested in 1992 apart from the two men, the two brothers that you've just named?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to see whether I still understand what it is about. The witness said: That's why they were taken to prison, that is, because they were Muslims. And your next question after Mr. Crncalo had said that he had gone to the police station and intervened, that they were released. The next question was: That's not true. Your two arrested cousins were taken to the central prison in Sarajevo. What is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour. I had made an unwarranted assumption there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That they were at the police station rather than in the prison.
